label: Matt Baxter 1/3: praise that backfires (parents)
theme: why outcome praise knocks confidence, and what to praise instead
coverQuestion: Should you tell them they were the *best* player?
coverContext: Mindset coach Matt Baxter on praise that backfires

qas.q: What's wrong with "you were the best"?
qas.a: "You were the best player out there" feels lovely, but it teaches a child that their worth depends on *results*.

qas.q: So what should I praise?
qas.a: Praise effort, choices and *courage* instead … "I loved how you kept demanding the ball after that missed chance."

qas.q: What else knocks their confidence?
qas.a: When parents step in too quickly, the child never gets to discover that they can *cope*.

quote: On the day they're not the best, the *confidence* goes with it.

caption:
"You were the best player out there" feels like the kindest thing to say after a game.

label: Matt Baxter 2/3: players who've stopped improving (coaches)
theme: plateaus are normal; how to get a stalled player learning again
coverQuestion: How do you help a player who's stopped *improving*?
coverContext: Mindset coach Matt Baxter on players who've stalled

qas.q: Why do some players get stuck?
qas.a: Ability is usually still developing underneath. What turns a plateau into a problem is how the child *interprets* it.

qas.q: What's the simplest tool?
qas.a: One of the simplest tools I use is the word *YET*. "I can't beat that defender" becomes "I can't beat that defender yet."

qas.q: What helps day to day?
qas.a: Pick one *specific* thing to work on for the next few weeks and notice small wins.

label: Matt Baxter 3/3: bouncing back from a mistake (parents)
theme: why some kids spiral after one mistake, and what they do instead
coverQuestion: Why do some kids *crumble* after one mistake?
coverContext: Mindset coach Matt Baxter on bouncing back mid-game

qas.q: Is it about talent?
qas.a: It rarely comes down to talent. It comes down to what the child does with the *next* moment.

qas.q: What do the resilient ones know?
qas.a: Young players who bounce back have learned that a mistake is an event, not a *verdict* on them.

qas.q: How do they reset?
qas.a: Notice the mistake, let it go, and put all their focus on the very next thing they can *control*.

quote: From the touchline, a parent influences more than they *realise*, mostly through their body language.

label: Paul Barry 1/3: is Category 1 always best? (parents)
theme: why the top category isn't automatically the right academy, and development centres as a way in
coverQuestion: Is a Category 1 academy always the *best* move?
coverContext: Ex-Arsenal and Crystal Palace coach Paul Barry on choosing an academy

qas.q: Is Category 1 right for every player?
qas.a: every player's journey is *different*, and therefore it's not a "one size fits all" development approach.

qas.q: What can a lower category club give?
qas.a: Sometimes, registering for a lower category club develops more humility, *resilience* and greater inner drive and motivation.

qas.q: Are development centres a real way in?
qas.a: Both Southend United and Crystal Palace had, or have, very productive development centres … which genuinely gave boys *opportunities* to trial throughout each season.

quote: Some players embrace the *pressure* and challenges posed by a Premier League Category 1 academy

label: Paul Barry 2/3: what parents should focus on (parents)
theme: the parent's job in the early years: support, leave the coaching, stop comparing, and release isn't the end
coverQuestion: What should parents focus on in the *early* years?
coverContext: Paul Barry, former Crystal Palace Foundation Phase head of coaching

qas.q: What's the parent's job?
qas.a: they need to be there emotionally for their child, give encouragement and positive reinforcement, and, importantly, leave the *coaching* to the club's coaches.

qas.q: What should parents stop doing?
qas.a: The life lessons formed through these experiences should be where parents focus, rather than constantly *comparing* their child with others

qas.q: And if they get released?
qas.a: a release shouldn't be thought of as the final moment in a young player's journey, but instead a crucial *learning* moment

quote: There are likely to be far more challenging and difficult moments compared to relative *successes*

label: Paul Barry 3/3: academy players at grassroots (coaches)
theme: U9-U11 academy players are allowed to keep playing grassroots, and why hardly anyone does
coverQuestion: Signed by an academy. Can they still play for *you*?
coverContext: Paul Barry of Football DNA on academy and grassroots football together

qas.q: Can academy players still play grassroots?
qas.a: The Premier League allows boys in academies from the age of U9s, U10s and U11s to play *grassroots* at the same time as academy football.

qas.q: Why is that allowed?
qas.a: to give the youngest players opportunities to retain *friendships* … and continue playing the game for social reasons.

qas.q: So why don't more families do it?
qas.a: hardly any parents that I've seen take up this opportunity, probably through fear of "losing *face*"

label: Girls United 1/3: what coaches look for (parents)
theme: the qualities beyond technical ability that coaches look for in young girls, and what the most improved players share
coverQuestion: What do coaches *really* look for in girls?
coverContext: The Girls United team on what matters beyond skill

qas.q: What do coaches look for beyond skill?
qas.a: Coaches want players who have a willingness to *learn*, who are focused, and who pay attention.

qas.q: What else matters?
qas.a: A growth mindset matters a lot, as does being able to take *feedback* and actually put it into practice.

qas.q: Who improves the most?
qas.a: The players who improve most tend to show real *determination*, they keep working even when a session is hard or they're not getting it right straight away.

quote: That combination of determination, communication and a genuine willingness to learn is what we see driving the biggest *improvements*.

label: Girls United 2/3: talented but not confident (parents)
theme: a talented daughter who lacks confidence: work on it with the coach, and don't coach from the sideline
coverQuestion: She's *talented*. So why is she holding back?
coverContext: The Girls United team on confidence in young girls

qas.q: Will confidence come if she keeps turning up?
qas.a: Confidence doesn't just build on its own from *showing* up

qas.q: So what can a parent do?
qas.a: Talk to her coach about it, as they can help build a purposeful *plan* to develop her confidence rather than leaving it to chance.

qas.q: What's the most common parent mistake?
qas.a: A big one is coaching from the *sideline*. It can contradict what the coach is asking for and distract the player

label: Girls United 3/3: why girls don't start or stay (coaches)
theme: the less obvious barriers that stop girls starting or staying, and what a good girls' club does about it
coverContext: The Girls United team on the barriers coaches don't see

qas.q: What's the barrier behind the practical ones?
qas.a: *Confidence* is often the real barrier underneath the practical ones

qas.q: What does that look like?
qas.a: some girls feel self-conscious about starting something new or don't have anyone in their family or *community* who plays.

qas.q: And girls new to sport?
qas.a: girls with no sporting background can feel like they're already *behind* before they start.

qas.q: What does a good girls' club do?
qas.a: Extra opportunities off the pitch, like events and activities that bring players and *families* together, are a good sign too.
